title: Connection throttling and graceful degradation for multi-region stores
creator: Asha Menon
description:
Summary: This ticket implements an adaptive connection-throttling and graceful-degradation layer for downstream state stores (Redis, Kafka producers/consumers, and primary DB) across multi-region deployments. The goal is to keep critical inference paths alive under downstream strain while preserving customer SLOs and predictable error-budget consumption.

Motivation:
- Recent incidents showed cascading failures when Redis or the regional DB experienced saturation, causing request timeouts and client-visible errors.
- We need a standardized strategy for connection pooling backpressure, circuit breakers, and tiered load shedding that applies consistently across hosted/dedicated/private modes.

SLOs & Error Budget Policy:
- Platform-critical endpoints (inference request acceptance): Availability >= 99.95% monthly, P99 tail latency < 150ms under normal load.
- Degradation targets: During a downstream outage, preserve at least 95% of successful request acceptance by returning degraded-but-valid responses (stale-cache or simplified scoring) before failing.
- Error budget burn triggers automated rollout halts and escalations at 25% and 75% burn rates.

Design overview (high level):
1) Connection pooling improvements:
   - Introduce an adaptive max-connections parameter per upstream per region. Base allocation + dynamic token-bucket reclamation when latency rises.
   - Add pool-level queue depth limits and FIFO overflow rejection to avoid head-of-line blocking.
   - Expose pool metrics: active_conns, queued_requests, conn_wait_ms_p95.

2) Circuit breakers & progressive backoff:
   - Failure thresholds: open CB when error rate > 5% and avg latency > 2x baseline for 30s.
   - Half-open probing uses low-QPS test traffic bound to <1% of baseline to avoid flapping.
   - Distinguish errors: transient timeouts vs terminal auth/403s (immediate open).

3) Load-shedding / graceful degradation policies:
   - Tiered response: (a) Best-effort full response, (b) Stale cached response (TTL policy & provenance header), (c) Reduced feature set (skip non-critical enrichment like semantic reranking), (d) Hard reject.
   - Per-customer priority: enterprise customers get prioritized tokens; free-tier uses lower priority queue. Priorities are configurable by route.
   - Soft-quota for background tasks (embeddings, async re-ranking) that will be paused under sustained downstream backpressure.

4) Multi-region failover orchestration:
   - Smart routing: when regional store latency/CBs exceed threshold, route reads to healthy region replicas using preference order and affinity.
   - Writes: failover-on-write only when synchronous replication is available; otherwise, reject with clear error advising retry or queueing.

5) Kafka consumer-side strategies:
   - Pause/resume partitions based on processing backlog and downstream health; maintain consumer-group rebalances minimal.
   - Use local circuit-breaker per consumer thread to avoid global stoppage.

Acceptance criteria:
- Unit and integration tests for pool limits, CB state transitions, and load-shedding fallback paths.
- Staging load test: under simulated Redis P95 latency of 1s, platform must keep inference-acceptance availability >= 99% with at least 90% degraded responses (stale or partial).
- Observability: dashboards for pool metrics, CB states, shed-rate, and customer-impact heatmap. Alerting at 5% shed-rate sustained for 2 minutes or CB flapping > 3 transitions in 5 minutes.

Rollout plan:
- Feature-flagged rollout: start with internal traffic only (10% of host region) -> expanded canary across multiple regions -> global rollout.
- Gradual increase of pool-throttle aggressiveness across flags.
- Post-rollout 72-hour incident watch with on-call engineer and SRE present.

Trade-offs and open questions:
- Stronger shedding reduces visible errors but may hide downstream faults from monitoring; mitigated via explicit shed metrics and synthetic tests.
- Synchronous multi-region writes are expensive; conservative default is to reject cross-region writes unless configured per-customer.
- Complexity: per-customer priority increases config surface and testing matrix. We plan to roll out basic two-tier priority first.

Runbook (synthesized):
- Detection: Alert: shed-rate > 5% or platform-critical endpoint availability drop.
- Triage: Check pool metrics (conn_wait_ms_p95, queued_requests), CB dashboard (open/hysteresis), and regional latency heatmap.
- Mitigation steps:
  1) Toggle read-routing to fallback region via console quick-toggle (documented below).
  2) Increase pool timeouts for non-critical paths and enable conservative shedding flag.
  3) If Redis is root cause, fail open caches to deliver stale responses and disable non-essential enrichments.
- Post-mortem: Record root cause, exact error budget burn, and recommended knob changes into the incident ticket.

Links & artifacts:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Adaptive+Connection+Throttling+Design
- Staging runbook deck: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1sY-example-runbook
- Related PR (pool + CB library): https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-runtime/pull/4312
- Load test dashboard (Grafana): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/conn-throttle-loadtest

Notes for reviewers:
- Focus on the CB thresholds and the queue overflow policy. We prioritized preventing head-of-line blocking over maximizing throughput in single-instance scenarios.
- Validate multi-region routing affinity implications for data consistency with PM and security teams.

- SRE to prepare canary gating rules and Grafana dashboards (blocked until PR merges).
- PM to confirm customer priority tiers and default policies by 2026-03-05.
